overview: Long QT syndrome is a cardiac electrical disorder characterized by delayed ventricular repolarization resulting in a prolonged QT interval on ECG. The condition increases the risk of dangerous ventricular arrhythmias, particularly torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, syncope, seizures, and sudden cardiac death. Long QT syndrome may be inherited or acquired through medications, electrolyte disturbances, or other medical conditions.
ecg_clues: QTc greater than 440 ms in men
QTc greater than 460 ms in women
QTc greater than 500 ms indicates high arrhythmia risk
ecg_limitations: accurate QT measurement requires clear T-wave termination
QT interval varies with heart rate
single beat measurements may be inaccurate
ECG alone cannot distinguish congenital versus acquired LQTS
ECG alone cannot identify genetic subtype
risk_factors: family history of long QT syndrome
family history of sudden cardiac death
complications: brain injury from prolonged cardiac arrest

history_questions: Do symptoms occur after sudden noises or startling events?
Has anyone in your family died suddenly at a young age?
Has anyone in your family been diagnosed with long QT syndrome?
Are you taking medications known to prolong QT interval?
Have you recently experienced severe vomiting or diarrhea?

prevention: screen family members when inherited disease is suspected
when_to_seek_help: known long QT with worsening symptoms

followup_questions.syncope: Have you fainted recently or in the past?
followup_questions.seizure_history: Have you ever had unexplained seizures?
followup_questions.family_history_sudden_death: Has anyone in your family died suddenly at a young age?
followup_questions.electrolyte_status: Have you recently had severe vomiting, diarrhea, or abnormal electrolyte tests?
followup_questions.medication_list: Are you taking any antibiotics, antidepressants, antiarrhythmics, or other medications?

confidence_rules: QTc greater than 440 ms in men increases suspicion
QTc greater than 460 ms in women increases suspicion
QTc greater than 500 ms strongly increases risk
family history of sudden death strongly increases confidence
torsades de pointes strongly supports diagnosis
drug exposure increases acquired LQTS confidence
electrolyte abnormalities increase acquired LQTS confidence
agent_reasoning_hints: QTc greater than 500 ms is associated with increased torsades risk
torsades de pointes is the hallmark life threatening arrhythmia of LQTS
not all prolonged QT intervals represent congenital disease
electrolyte abnormalities should always be investigated
drug induced QT prolongation may be reversible
recurrent unexplained syncope should raise suspicion
sudden unexplained drowning may suggest inherited LQTS
source_notes: QT interval represents ventricular depolarization and repolarization
Bazett formula is the most commonly used QT correction formula
QTc greater than 500 ms is associated with increased torsades risk
Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia can prolong QT interval
Myocardial ischemia may cause moderate QT prolongation
Long QT syndrome may present as unexplained syncope or seizures

Family history of sudden death is an important diagnostic clue
